extracted.intended_audience: screenwriters and narrative writers (novelists, playwrights) learning story craft
extracted.subtask_description: Practical principles for designing cinematic stories and scenes: how to build scenes beat-by-beat, create an Inciting Incident, shape a Spine (through-line), design cast and setting, and achieve authenticity and emotional energy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fine writing emphasizes reactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Fine writing puts less stress on what happens than on to whom it happens and why and how it happens; the richest pleasures focus on the reactions events cause and the insight gained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate scenes by how imaginatively and insightfully characters react to events rather than by the mere occurrence of events. Examples: genre conventions supply expected events (lovers meet, detective discovers a crime) — the craft is in the reactions. Anti-pattern: scenes where expectation equals result and reactions lack imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action–Reaction–Gap (the gap) as the substance and energy of story
rubrics_metrics.description: The substance of story is the gap that splits open between what a human being expects to happen when he takes an action and what really does happen; this rift (probability vs. necessity) is also the source of story energy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design scenes to create and enlarge gaps between expectation and outcome; each opening of the gap is an emotional charge for audience empathy ('Oh, my God!', 'Oh, no!'). Use the gap to ignite audience reaction and drive scene momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beat-by-beat construction: build dynamic series of action/reaction gaps
rubrics_metrics.description: A scene should be imagined and written beat by beat, gap by gap: a dynamic series of action/reaction/gap, renewed action/surprising reaction/gap builds the scene to and around its Turning Point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write scenes as a chain of beats where each reaction surprises and advances emotional truth. Example: CHINATOWN knocks/blocks/insult/barging/confession sequence. Anti-pattern: 'dead seconds' — beats where nothing meaningful happens; editors will cut scenes where expectation simply equals result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pointless pace killers
rubrics_metrics.description: Any scene in which reactions lack insight and imagination, forcing expectation to equal result, is a 'pointless pace killer.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trim or rework beats that merely show routine or predictable outcomes with no revealing reaction. Example anti-pattern: a character knocks and is politely admitted — eight dead seconds of no dramatic value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vivid, lucid description to immerse reader/audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Words are a medium: write vivid descriptions so that when someone reads your pages he will, beat by beat, gap by gap, live through the roller coaster you experienced at your desk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure prose by its ability to allow the reader/viewer to 'plunge into each gap' and feel the physical/emotional responses (pulse, laughter, tears). Clarity and vividness are means, not ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inciting Incident must be dynamic and fully developed
rubrics_metrics.description: The Inciting Incident, the first major event of the telling, must be a dynamic, fully developed event (not static or vague) that radically upsets the balance of forces in the protagonist's life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the opening major event decisively changes the protagonist's equilibrium and clearly signals that life is out of balance. Anti-pattern: vague premise statements or anemic life-change (e.g., 'she's bored; she moves to L.A.' with no consequential upset).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inciting Incident produces immediate awareness and desire to restore balance
rubrics_metrics.description: When an Inciting Incident occurs the protagonist is immediately aware (or soon becomes aware) that life is out of balance and is aroused to desire to restore that balance — conceiving an Object of Desire and actively pursuing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the Inciting Incident spawns a conscious objective (and often an unconscious one) that propels action. The protagonist's pursuit of the Object of Desire should follow naturally from the upset.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inciting Incident may require setup and prompt payoff without undue delay
rubrics_metrics.description: Occasionally an Inciting Incident needs two events (setup and payoff). If logic requires a setup, the writer cannot delay the payoff for long and keep the protagonist ignorant of the imbalance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check pacing: if a setup is shown, ensure payoff follows soon enough for the protagonist (and audience) to recognize that life has changed. Example: JAWS setup (shark eats swimmer) then payoff (sheriff discovers corpse). Anti-pattern: long sequences that ignore the consequence of the setup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protagonist must react (refusal can be a reaction but cannot last)
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist must respond to the Inciting Incident. A refusal to act is a valid reaction but cannot be permanent — the drive to restore sovereignty over existence compels eventual pursuit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge character reactions for appropriateness to character and world; a refusal is acceptable as long as it serves the story and doesn't stall action indefinitely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects of Desire — conscious and unconscious desires
rubrics_metrics.description: The Inciting Incident arouses a conscious Object of Desire and often an unconscious one; complex protagonists feel both, and these desires may be in direct conflict (conscious vs. unconscious).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify both layers of desire in the protagonist. Stories driven by unconscious desire are richer and allow conscious goals to change while the deeper drive (the 'unconscious') remains the Spine. Examples: CARNAL KNOWLEDGE (conscious search for perfect woman vs. unconscious desire to degrade).

rubrics_metrics.name: The Spine (Through-line/Superobjective) unifies design
rubrics_metrics.description: The Spine is the deep desire and effort by the protagonist to restore balance; it is the primary unifying force that holds all scenes, images, and words together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether all scenes relate causally or thematically to the Spine. If no unconscious desire exists, the conscious objective becomes the Spine (e.g., Bond: 'to defeat the arch-villain'). The Spine must be durable and consistent; if it collapses, the story falls apart.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting: period, duration, location, and level of conflict — fill with saturated detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Setting is framed by period, duration, location, and level of conflict; to tell an original, cliché-free story you must fill that frame with a depth and breadth of detail (research to saturation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use research to populate setting with rituals, work-life, politics (power structures), meals, values, genres, biographies — those details generate atmosphere and authenticity. Once saturated, a unique voice/atmosphere emerges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Backstory as significant events (not mere biography)
rubrics_metrics.description: Backstory is the set of significant past events the writer can use to build the story's progressions; it is not simply life history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether past events included are those that materially inform present choices and plot progressions — plant events the writer can 'harvest' later rather than dumping exhaustive biographies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cast design: polarization and purposeful roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing in a work of art is accidental; each character must fit a purpose and the first principle of cast design is polarization — roles should have contrasting attitudes so each reacts distinctively and supplies conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess cast to ensure no two characters share the same attitude (if they do, collapse or remove one). Polarization maximizes scene opportunities and conflict (Jeffrey family example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial knowledge, authority, and authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: A true author is an artist with godlike knowledge of subject; the proof of authorship is that pages 'smack of authority.' Authority produces authenticity — an internally consistent world the audience can believe in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rate the writer's demonstrated knowledge of subject and whether that knowledge yields credible character behavior, convincing cause-and-effect, and an internally consistent fictional reality. Authenticity may favor a convincing impossibility over an unconvincing actuality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telling detail and economy of detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Authenticity depends on the 'telling detail': a few selected details allow the audience's imagination to supply the rest and complete a credible whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer specific, evocative details over exhaustive literalism. Beware of overdoing realism (esp. sex/violence) — too much or too explicit can shatter credibility and yank the audience out of the story. Example positive: ALIEN's small collectibles making crew feel like truck drivers; example negative: gratuitous hyperreal sex/violence that feels staged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality emerges from mastery and authenticity, not eccentricity
rubrics_metrics.description: Originality lies in the struggle for authenticity, not in eccentric self-consciousness; personal style is a natural effect of an author mastering subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge originality by whether it arises from deep research and authentic choices rather than forced oddity. Compare different authors' voices as products of their mastery rather than mere gimmicks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of multiple POVs to reveal new emotional truths
rubrics_metrics.description: After creating an honest moment from one point of view, move around the universe into other points of view (even the inanimate) to find unexpected reactions, then return to the original mind to discover a new emotional truth by asking 'If I were this character under these new circumstances, what would I do?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether shifting POVs in a scene yields surprising reactions and deeper emotional truths. Use the technique to splinter expectation/result gaps and to test opposites ('And what is the opposite of that?').
